items.title: Unpacking Ethical, Privacy, And Governance Risks in AI-IoT Based Healthcare Environments: A thematic analysis
items.abstract: Objective: The paper aimed to examine ethical, privacy, and governance challenges in AI-IoT (Artificial Intelligence-based Internet of Things) healthcare environments. Design: A total of 39 peer-reviewed open-access studies were screened and used for a systematic review using the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) framework. A multi-stage thematic analysis was used for identifying recurring patterns within the literature and answering the research questions. Results/outcomes: The identified challenges in the AI-IoT healthcare ecosystems, arising from the thematic analysis, are privacy and continuous surveillance, algorithmic bias and lack of explainability, limitations for informed consent, and fragmented governance and accountability. Conclusion: The findings, in sync with STS theory, indicate that challenges in AI-IoT healthcare systems cannot be addressed solely through technological innovations. In response, the study proposed an Integrated Human-Centric Trust Framework to integrate human intervention with technological advancements.

items.title: Use of Artificial Intelligence among Undergraduate Medical Students at Dhaka National Medical College: A Descriptive Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Background: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly increasing among university students worldwide. However, little is known about how undergraduate medical students in Bangladesh engage with AI tools in their education. Objective: To assess the pattern of using AI and the self-reported knowledge and attitude regarding AI among undergraduate medical students of Dhaka National Medical College (DNMC). Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 5th-year MBBS students of DNMC from December 2025 to July 2026 (4th-year students were excluded). By convenience type of non-probability sampling, 125 medical students completed a structured, self-administered questionnaire distributed as a Google Form through students' WhatsApp number. The questionnaire included sociodemographic data, patterns of AI use, and a 10-item, 5-point Likert scale for assessment of self-reported knowledge and attitudes (range 10 to 50). Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, the chi-square test, independent t-test, and ANOVA; p<0.05 was considered significant. Results: Mean age of 125 students was 21.7±1.7 years, among them 56.0% were female. Almost all respondents (97.6%) were familiar with AI. Most of them (89.6%) were current users, most commonly of ChatGPT (81.2%) and Gemini (32.1%). Majority of them (81.3%) thought that AI would be beneficial to their future career and 74.2% felt it should be taught to all medical students, 41.1% felt confident about replacement of medical specialities. Half of respondents (50.0%) were concerned about AI-generated misinformation, and 79.3% reported at least occasional difficulty verifying AI-generated academic content. The composite knowledge–attitude score (mean 37.2±6.0 of 50) rose significantly with academic year (p=0.023, driven by a 1st- versus 5th-year difference). Gender and current AI-use status were not significantly associated with the score. Conclusion: Most of the undergraduate medical students of DNMC have familiarity with use AIs and positive attitudes of it use for their learning. However, some of them are concerned about the misinformation may be produced by the AIs. Hence, structured AI-literacy training, from the first year of the MBBS curriculum, is a demand of the time. items.abstract: Background: Undergraduate healthcare students in India experience heavy academic pressure and exhausting hospital duties, yet rarely consult mental health professionals because of social stigma and fear of losing internal marks. Many students now turn to smartphone artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots late at night for private emotional comfort. This study assessed the prevalence of AI chatbot usage for emotional support, user perception, and emotional reliance among healthcare trainees in rural South India.

items.title: Using Generative AI for Behavioural Research Effectively and Responsibly: a BR-UK Statement
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used across the behavioural research lifecycle. It may improve the efficiency and quality of research, but rapid, uncritical adoption carries risks to research integrity: algorithmic bias, ethical concerns around consent, privacy and plagiarism, erosion of researchers’ skills and public trust, and environmental costs. This Open Letter presents Behavioural Research UK’s (BR-UK) statement on using generative AI effectively and responsibly in behavioural research. It was informed by existing guidance and expert consultation. The statement sets out BR-UK’s four key propositions: (1) research ethics and integrity principles must include AI concerns; (2) AI should assist, but not replace, researchers through a human-in-the-loop approach; (3) rigorous evaluation of AI use is essential; and (4) coordinated stakeholder action is needed to move from identifying risks to practical solutions. It then provides recommendations and points to practical tools, such as decision aids and checklists for declaring AI use, for seven stakeholder groups, namely research-generating institutions, funders, publication outlets, behavioural research networks and communities, AI platform and tool providers, individual researchers, and research users. The statement will be reviewed annually until 2028, the duration of BR-UK, as technology and evidence evolve.

items.title: Versioned Governance for Frontier AI: A Software-Engineering-Inspired Approach
items.abstract: Abstract Background FrontierAI laboratories govern deployed systems via model specifications, usage policies, and safety frameworks. These governance documents undergo repeated revisions, yet current practices rarely distinguish substantive normative policy changes from mere editorial clarifications. This produces silent drift: continuous normative modification without clear documentation of changes, reasons for modification, and the institutional authority under which changes were made. The following are examples of an AI API that identifies new drugs and vaccines for a given disease, scaling from a simple “Name that drug!” function to much more advanced models. This paper reviews the revision histories for five publicly available AI governance instruments that are slated for release between 2019 and 2025; OpenAI usage policies and Model Specific, Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. This paper identifies the areas where current practices seemed aligned with formal versioning discipline, and it pinpointed the areas where there are persistent implementation gaps. Version number tracking vocabulary is becoming more frequent at the whole document level, while the specific term level is still not being used. The type of AI disruptive technology that incites a substantial shift from a normative route is an exogenous shock. Current changelogs are descriptive, but they are not change classified. Explicit structural rollback mechanisms are not found in any of the examined instruments. Through this analysis, we realize that there are genuine limits of the software-as-a-policy analogy, taking these limitations as hard design constraints for possible AI regulation instead of unconsidered counter-arguments. Implications: AI labs can “self-engineer” a lightweight globally adaptable, versioning approach to formally defined meta-changes, clause granular history logs, design rollback aware implementations, and misclassification preserved as independently audit-bounded events that can be independently audited by regulators/independent auditors and formally accepted by regulators as an independent practice. Does not imply specific compelling AI system substantive policy content.

items.title: Von menschzentrierter KI zu nachhaltigen autonomen Systemen: eine soziotechnische Forschungs- und Entwicklungsagenda
items.abstract: Der Beitrag entwickelt aus den Erfahrungen des Projekts Künstlich Menschlich Intelligent eine soziotechnische Forschungs- und Entwicklungsagenda für die nächste Phase der digitalen und nachhaltigen Transformation (Twin Transformation). Im Zentrum steht die Frage, unter welchen Bedingungen datenbasierte Technologien und insbesondere KI-Agenten und autonome Systeme zu humangerechter Arbeit, Effizienz, organisationaler Wertschöpfung und Nachhaltigkeit beitragen können. Ausgehend von einem Dreiklang aus Wirkung, Gestaltung und Befähigung wird gezeigt, dass die nächste Welle der digitalen Transformation nicht als lineare technische Implementierung verstanden werden kann, sondern als reflexiver Gestaltungsprozess, in dem Mensch, Technik und Organisation gemeinsam unter dem Leitbild der Nachhaltigkeit weiterentwickelt werden. Die Projekterfahrungen und aktuelle Erkenntnisse machen zentrale Ambivalenzen sichtbar: Digitalisierung bedeutet nicht automatisch KI-Readiness; niedrigschwellige KI-Nutzung ersetzt keine organisationale Gestaltungsfähigkeit; und Entlastung durch KI kann zugleich Arbeitsverdichtung, Verantwortungsverschiebung oder De-Skilling erzeugen. Darauf aufbauend formuliert der Beitrag zukünftige Forschungsfelder zu mehrdimensionaler Wirkungsmessung, Mensch-KI-Interaktion, Human-AI Teaming, Ko-Adaption, Partizipation, KI-Governance, Verantwortlichkeit, Aufsicht, Kompetenzentwicklung, Transfer, digitaler Souveränität, Abhängigkeiten und Lock-in-Effekten. Besondere Aufmerksamkeit gilt kleinen und mittleren Unternehmen sowie ressourcenbeschränkten Organisationen, die für nachhaltige KI-Nutzung Orientierungswissen, Methoden, Demonstratoren und intermediäre Transferstrukturen benötigen.

items.title: When Assistance Becomes Infrastructure
items.abstract: Debates about the future of artificial intelligence often focus on a single decisive moment, when machines surpass humans. This essay examines a less visible path: AI may become infrastructure through a series of local, reasonable decisions that no one makes as a whole. We follow one question across three stages: can we still go back? First, services are redesigned around AI and non-AI channels close, a form of coercion without a coercer. Second, the human role shifts from producing to ratifying, and the skills needed to check AI output erode, as early clinical and labor-market evidence suggests. Third, the ability to compare work with and without AI disappears, so that a society may lose not only a capability but also the knowledge that it existed. A simple model shows how two reinforcing loops create hysteresis, in which the way back costs more than the way in. We then discuss brakes (laws, fallback options, reserves of skill), structural forcings (public debt, the decline of public research, geopolitical rivalry), and four possible end states: integration, bypass, managed coexistence, and partial return. We argue that the key question is whether human alternatives remain reproducible and measurable.

items.title: When Does GenAI Use Support Critical Thinking? A Cross-Cultural Structural Account of Transactive Memory with GenAI
items.abstract: Whether generative AI (GenAI) use helps or hinders critical thinking remains contested, and existing accounts emphasize exposure to the tool rather than how a person structures their engagement with it. Extending Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) theory to human-AI partnerships, we test a structural account of critical thinking in GenAI-assisted academic work among 891 college students in the United States and Türkiye. Self-appraised thinking ability and confidence in the partnership shaped how much practical experience a person built up with GenAI, but neither predicted critical thinking directly. That experience mattered only through two downstream behaviors, dividing and coordinating cognitive labor with the tool, and actively reworking its output rather than accepting it as given. A multigroup comparison found this structure largely invariant, with two theoretically interpretable exceptions. This study offers a structural, TMS-based account of critical thinking in GenAI-assisted work.

items.title: When Employees Perceive AI as a Partner: How Human–Machine Relationship Perception Shapes Employee Innovative Behavior
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into organizational work, highlighting the importance of employees’ relational perceptions of AI for innovative behavior. Drawing on cognitive appraisal and social exchange theories, this study examines how human–machine relationship perception (HMRP) influences employee innovative behavior through psychological empowerment, with perceived organizational support as a moderator. Three-wave, multi-source data were collected from 428 employee–supervisor dyads across 27 technology-intensive firms. Results indicate that HMRP positively predicts innovative behavior (β = 0.360, p < 0.001) and psychological empowerment (β = 0.470, p < 0.001). Psychological empowerment positively predicts innovative behavior (β = 0.320, p < 0.001) and mediates the HMRP–innovation relationship (indirect effect = 0.150, 95% CI [0.108, 0.198]), explaining 41.7% of the total effect. Perceived organizational support strengthens the HMRP–empowerment relationship (β = 0.130, p = 0.001), with conditional indirect effects increasing from 0.109 to 0.192 and a moderated mediation index of 0.042 (95% CI [0.018, 0.071]). These findings extend human–AI collaboration research by identifying relational cognition and psychological empowerment as mechanisms linking AI collaboration to employee innovation and highlighting the importance of organizational support.

items.title: When Machines Mislead: Trust, Cognitive Processing, and Belief in AI-Labeled Misinformation
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has increased the speed and scale at which plausible text and other media can be produced, raising questions about how people evaluate information explicitly attributed to AI. This integrative narrative review brings together research on misinformation judgments, online credibility cues, trust in automation, dual-process accounts of reasoning, and Need for Cognition (NFC). The literature suggests that people may use source labels as one cue among several when judging credibility, while trust in AI can shape willingness to rely on AI-generated information. Analytic reasoning is associated with better discrimination between true and false news, but NFC is a motivational disposition toward effortful thinking and should not be treated as a direct measure of analytic ability or heuristic use. Evidence also cautions against assuming that AI disclosure uniformly increases or decreases credibility: outcomes may depend on the message, the source cue, prior expectations, and the task. The review proposes a cautious framework in which AI attribution is interpreted through individual beliefs about AI and evaluated alongside message-level evidence. Direct evidence on the joint roles of trust in AI and NFC in responses to AI-labeled misinformation remains limited. Future research should measure perceived accuracy and truth discernment separately, distinguish source trust from message accuracy, and test these relationships across culturally diverse samples, including India.

items.title: YouMii: A Daily Companion App for Mental Well-Being
items.abstract: Mental health disorders such as depression, anxiety, and chronic stress have caused widespread global concerns, necessitating innovative, accessible, and scalable intervention strategies. With advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), natural language processing (NLP), and affective computing, there is growing potential to develop emotionally intelligent systems that offer personalized mental health support. This research presents the analysis, design and development of a positive-psychology-Gemini-based mobile AI companion application, YouMii, aimed at promoting general well-being, and encouraging proactive self-care via empathetic support and context-aware conversational interactions/interventions. Through mood-based and behavioural tracking, contextual reasoning is developed and recommendations are suggested. Findings indicate that empathetic support (e.g., mood trackers, self-reflection journaling), learnability, accuracy and relevance e.g., reminders, progress reports/insights may complement conventional therapy. Examples of scenarios and rules for human-AI co-design of therapy conclude.

items.title: A Deep Learning-Based Marker Augmentation Model for Markerless Motion Tracking During Manual Lifting
items.abstract: Computer vision is increasingly used to extract movement data from videos and perform ergonomic analyses. However, open-source computer vision algorithms often only detect major body keypoints, which are insufficient to calculate three-dimensional (3D) joint kinematics. This study developed a deep learning marker-augmentation model to predict the 3D positions of 33 anatomical markers from 20 video keypoints, along with participant height and weight, and lifting style. Data for model training and testing were collected from 21 adults performing lifting tasks recorded simultaneously using an optical motion capture system and smartphone cameras. Both video keypoints and predicted anatomical markers were used to drive inverse kinematic analysis. The mean kinematic error decreased from 18.5° to 9.5° when inverse kinematics was driven by augmented markers compared to using original video keypoints. These findings suggest that marker augmentation can improve video-based kinematic analysis and may support biomechanical evaluation of lifting tasks outside laboratory settings.

items.title: A Simulation Testbed for Self-Governing Human-Machine Institutions
items.abstract: AI agents no longer act alone: they cooperate, coordinate and compete within and between groups, increasingly alongside humans who are in, on or out of ``the loop''. Whether such mixed groups can govern themselves is an open question about machine behaviour and human-computer interaction that needs a testbed for hybrid institutions. We present Megabike, a multi-agent simulator and serious game with interdependent arenas for common-pool resource management, cooperative survival and constitutional choice. Riders sharing a megabike must agree their arrangements for steering, pedalling and distributing resources, and their political regime, while negotiating with rival bikes and avoiding an existential threat. Every rule is enforced by the simulator, every action is logged, and any seat can be taken by a human or a machine, so governance can be studied under well-defined metrics. We demonstrate Megabike with forty sessions in which language-model riders with cooperative, lazy, subversive or opposing dispositions chose regimes, elected leaders and expelled one another. The results show that different combinations of agent archetypes could produce unexpected and counterproductive outcomes. We conclude with extensions for systematic experiments mixing human and computational agents.

items.title: A Structured Mixed-Methods Workflow for User-Centred Digital Mental Health Platform Design
items.abstract: Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) frequently experience low user engagement and high attrition, highlighting the importance of incorporating user-centred design approaches during early-stage development. This study presents a structured mixed-methods workflow that integrates participatory co-design activities with a complementary quantitative prototype evaluation to support the formative development of digital mental health platforms. Using a qualitatively driven sequential design with an embedded quantitative strand, 45 university students in design, engineering, architecture and ergonomics programmes took part in three participatory co-design workshops in nine groups of five and, at the close of the final session, each group rated the low-fidelity AMGR-I prototype it had itself built against eleven design criteria. Ratings differed systematically across criteria (Friedman χ2(10) = 225.73, p < 0.001, Kendall’s W = 0.50), and the difference persisted when the clustering of ratings within the nine artefacts was modelled. Gamification was rated significantly lower than every other criterion after Holm’s correction and content quality highest, while data privacy and security was among the lowest-rated criteria despite being one of the most frequently and forcefully discussed concerns in the workshops. Because the instrument measured evaluation of the artefact rather than the importance attached to each criterion, that pattern is a convergence between the two strands rather than a paradox: the requirement these participants discussed most was the one their own artefacts served worst. That convergence is the study’s central integrated finding. The participants are characterised throughout as design-literate formative evaluators rather than as prospective users, and the resulting design propositions are presented as hypotheses for subsequent testing. The contribution of the paper is the workflow itself: a lightweight, low-cost and classroom-deployable procedure for combining co-design with structured prototype evaluation at the pre-clinical formative stage.

items.title: A systematic review examining conceptualizations and implementation pathways alongside empirical evidence of artificial intelligence literacy in higher education from 2021 to 2025
items.abstract: Through a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review of peer-reviewed publications (2021–2025), this study mapped the conceptualization, implementation pathways, and empirical evidence of AI literacy in higher education, drawing on a screened corpus of 56 peer-reviewed publications. Three research questions guided this review: (1) how AI literacy is conceptualized in higher education; (2) what effective pathways have been implemented for developing AI literacy among students and educators; and (3) what empirical evidence reveals about AI literacy levels, dimensions, and interdimensional relationships among students and educators. Findings reveal that conceptual fragmentation persists in definitions, frameworks, and dimensions (RQ1), with cognitive and behavioral dimensions more frequently emphasized than affective and ethical dimensions. This pattern is reflected in implementation pathways (RQ2), where many initiatives emphasize operational proficiency, tool use, and prompting, while critical reflection, ethical engagement, and longer-term developmental outcomes receive less consistent attention. Empirically (RQ3), student-focused studies commonly report moderate overall AI literacy, whereas educator-focused studies indicate readiness concerns in several higher-order, pedagogical, and ethical domains; because measures, samples, and contexts differ across studies, these findings should not be interpreted as a direct statistical comparison between populations. Several studies also indicate interrelationships among the four ABCE dimensions, behavioral engagement and ethical understanding mediated an affective-to-cognitive pathway. Taken together, the findings suggest the need to move beyond narrowly tool-oriented approaches toward theoretically grounded, dimensionally balanced, critically engaged, and longitudinally sustained AI-literacy development, with implications for higher-education policy, curriculum design, and professional development. items.title: A transparent crop model-driven and AI-assisted framework for agricultural decision support
items.abstract: Agricultural decision-making requires evaluation of complex interactions under variable environment and management conditions. Process-based crop models are widely used to support these decisions by providing scientifically grounded analysis of management alternatives. However, their application remains constrained by technical complexity and the difficulty of translating informal decision contexts into complete and reproducible model analyses without expert knowledge. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer opportunities to improve accessibility, but questions remain regarding transparency, reproducibility, trustworthiness, and the appropriate role of AI in scientific decision-support systems. We present Agricultural Large Language Model (AgriLLM), a transparent crop model-driven and AI-assisted framework for agricultural decision support that explicitly separates AI-assisted interpretation, deterministic decision processing, and scientific inference. A central feature of the framework is its target-driven design, in which decision objectives rather than user phrasing determine the information requirements, simulation design, and evaluation procedures needed to support decision-making. Using Agricultural Production Systems Simulator (APSIM) Next Generation as a proof-of-concept platform, we demonstrate the framework across cultivar selection, time of sowing, and nitrogen management scenarios. The results show how diverse and incomplete user inputs can be transformed into transparent and reproducible decision workflows while maintaining explicit representation of assumptions, evidence, and decision logic. The framework demonstrates how AI can be integrated with process-based crop modelling to improve accessibility and usability while preserving transparency, reproducibility, and scientific integrity in agricultural decision support.

items.title: Accountable Boundary Work Around Misinformation-Sharing Sources
items.abstract: Users encountering misinformation on social media must decide what to believe and also whether and how to manage an ongoing boundary with the source that shared it. We report a qualitative study with 29 participants from a university community, using an instrumented timeline environment to examine how they interpreted misinformation cues and source-level controls during feed browsing. The sources could retain value after sharing misinformation, and the content was not designed around ideological or identity conflict. Thus, acting on a source required a judgment of its own. We conceptualize deciding whether and how to alter that boundary as accountable boundary work . The framework distinguishes warrant assessment and proportional evaluation as two linked dimensions of judgment, with enactment concerning whether a contemplated boundary move can be carried through. Participants could recognize content as misinformation while preserving the existing source boundary. They also differentiated moves such as filtering and reporting according to whose exposure or relationship would change and whether platform authority could be invoked. Platform design shaped the grounds available for judgment, the interpretation of available controls, and whether contemplated moves were actionable in the flow of the feed. We contribute an interaction-grounded framework for source-level misinformation response, and design and governance implications for legible, socially defensible, and lower-burden boundary management.

items.title: Advisor, Co-pilot, or Guardian? AI Role Framing and Human Decision Behavior in Automated Vehicle Takeovers
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technology has gradually been integrated into automated vehicles. However, how this technology could systematically support takeover transitions in SAE Level 3 automated vehicles remains unknown, even though this level may remain a major form of driving automation in the near future. To address this, we implemented the three AI roles proposed by the triadic Human-AI collaboration framework (Advisor, Co-pilot, and Guardian) as potential authority-ability configurations for AI agents within an automated system. We then examined their interactions with explanation type (why and action) and directional semantics (ipsilateral and contralateral) in an automated driving simulator study with 24 participants. Results showed that, across the three AI roles, Advisor had the shortest decision-making time, followed by Guardian and Co-pilot. Advisor and Guardian were associated with higher decision-making accuracy and higher satisfaction ratings than Co-pilot. Guardian was associated with the lowest workload, followed by Advisor and Co-pilot. The effect of explanation type on decision-making time depended on AI role. Action explanations were faster under Advisor, whereas why explanations were faster under Co-pilot. For directional semantics, ipsilateral semantics were associated with shorter decision-making time than contralateral semantics. Overall, these findings provide preliminary guidance for designing AI-role authority-ability configurations and their associated speech-based takeover messages.

items.abstract: This reflective article critically examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents configured as educational tutors in secondary education. Based on a rigorous review of meta-analyses, international case studies, and specialized academic literature, it explores the conceptual foundations of intelligent tutoring and contemporary models of digital pedagogy. It examines real-world applications of intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), their benefits in terms of learning personalization, immediate feedback, student autonomy, and intrinsic motivation. Likewise, ethical challenges such as algorithmic bias, risks of dehumanizing educational processes, and vulnerabilities related to data privacy are identified. Finally, pedagogical guidelines are presented for the ethical and effective integration of AI agents in school settings, emphasizing teacher training, student-centered design, and continuous educational impact assessment.

items.title: AgentFail: A Stateful Paradigm for Quantifying Autonomous Agent Over-Reliance and Multi-Turn Operational Failures
items.abstract: Abstract As Large Language Models (LLMs) transition from passive text generators to autonomous AI agents executing multi-step workflows, evaluating their operational safety becomes a critical, unsolved bottleneck. Current evaluation frameworks heavily prioritize conversational fluency or static reasoning, completely ignoring the severe financial, legal, and operational risks of autonomous actions in live software environments. To bridge this critical gap, we introduce AgentFail, an open-source, turnkey benchmark engineered to evaluate agentic over-reliance and catastrophic failure modes across leading LLM architectures within Dockerized enterprise software environments (including Salesforce, Jira, and SQL-based ERP networks). Comprising 500 complex, multi-turn corporate task scenarios embedded with subtle operational edge cases and ambiguous constraints, AgentFail exposes a pervasive vulnerability in frontier architectures: current state-of-the-art reasoning models exhibit acute automation over-reliance, confidently executing destructive actions—such as unauthorized data deletion, critical financial ledger miscalculations, and privacy-violating data distributions—in over 42% of empirical trials without triggering built-in safety overrides or initiating human validation requests. We introduce a formal taxonomy of agentic failure alongside two novel continuous evaluation metrics: Error Propagation Velocity (Vep ) and the Over-Reliance Coefficient (Ω). By open-sourcing our entire testing infrastructure, automated environment wrappers, and baseline evaluation suite, we provide a rigorous, highly transferable safety baseline to accelerate the development of alignment strategies and guardrails for next-generation agentic workflows.

items.title: AI Resources in Higher Education: What Instructors Need and How We Deliver
items.abstract: Abstract As generative AI reshapes higher education, instructors across the globe have become increasingly interested in integrating AI into the classroom, but they require trusted, timely, and relevant resources for such integration. To enable the development of an open educational resource (OER) that could be remixed and adapted to different teaching contexts and support inclusive access, this study examined what instructors want and need from an open resource on AI in teaching and learning in higher education and documented a process for developing professional development resources in a time of rapid technological change. This study employed a multiphase mixed-methods design. First, a statewide needs assessment survey was conducted with 149 instructors to identify needs, challenges, and priorities across diverse institutional and disciplinary contexts. Participants prioritized three core content domains for the resource—AI literacy, pedagogical strategies, and ethics—and favored interactive, adaptable, and open resources grounded in practical classroom applications. These findings were used to develop an OER prototype, on which 75 instructors provided feedback, affirming the utility of the resource and suggesting areas for further refinement. This study contributes an educator-informed process for translating instructors’ needs into the design and formative evaluation of an adaptable, openly licensed faculty development resource. This evidence-based, educator-driven approach demonstrates how those tasked with faculty development on AI can develop and refine timely resources that meet the needs of educators from diverse contexts, offering a flexible, scalable, and community-oriented pathway for bridging institutional resource gaps and advancing inclusive faculty development in the age of AI.

items.title: AI-Assisted Business Analysis: Usability, Trust Cues, and Human Oversight in Responses to Under-Specified Requests
items.abstract: Analysts increasingly turn to generative AI assistants for business-analysis work, yet they often start with short prompts that carry no organizational context. We examined how three general-purpose assistants respond to such under-specified requests and what their responses imply for usability, trust and human oversight. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini each received five prompts that named only a common business-analysis task: requirements analysis, requirements prioritization, user-story generation, stakeholder-needs analysis and business-process improvement. Each prompt was run three times per system in fresh sessions on 24 and 25 September 2026, giving 45 outputs, which we coded for accuracy, completeness, internal consistency, usability, transparency and support for human oversight. ChatGPT and Gemini explained the named concept in all 30 of their outputs and never asked about the user's situation. Claude asked a clarifying question in 13 of its 15 outputs, and five of its outputs contained little or no task content. Gemini covered 59 of 60 checklist elements but accounted for five of the six accuracy issues. No output expressed uncertainty or suggested verification, and every substantive output was generic. The results point to a trade-off between immediate completeness and handing control back to the analyst. They support a workflow in which analysts supply context, check outputs and validate them with stakeholders before acting on them.

items.title: AI-giarism and Beyond: Mapping the Risks and Opportunities of Generative AI for Academic Integrity in Higher Education.
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has sparked urgent debate about its implications for traditional scholarly standards. This systematic literature review (SLR) investigates how GenAI impacts academic integrity in higher education, identifying specific risks to student honesty and emerging opportunities for pedagogical transformation. Following the PRISMA 2020 framework, 104 records were screened, yielding a final selection of 19 peer-reviewed articles published between 2023 and 2026. Data were synthesized using thematic analysis, and findings are categorized into three core themes: (1) Academic Integrity and the Evolution of Misconduct, (2) Policy and Institutional Strategy, and (3) Ethics and Educational Impact. The review identifies a persistent policy gap in higher education and a shift from traditional plagiarism to "AI-giarism." The impact of GenAI is found to be transformative rather than purely destructive: while it presents significant risks to current product-based assessments, it offers a critical opportunity to modernize education through AI literacy and process-based evaluation. The study concludes that academic integrity must transition from a policing-based model to an ethical partnership model between students and institutions.

items.title: An AI/generative AI-assisted blended learning intervention for nursing undergraduates: a quasi-experimental study of attitudes toward AI, AI literacy, and autonomous learning competency
items.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping healthcare, highlighting the need for nursing graduates to develop relevant competencies. However, structured AI education remains limited in nursing programs, and evidence on the effects of AI-focused teaching interventions remains scarce. Methods A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest study was conducted among 142 undergraduate nursing students at a university in southwestern Zhejiang, China. Seventy-two students participated in a 10-week AI/generative AI (GenAI)-assisted blended learning course comprising 12 h of self-paced online learning and 6 h of hands-on workshops, while 70 students received standard instruction. Attitudes toward AI, AI literacy, and autonomous learning competency were assessed before and immediately after the intervention using validated instruments. Post-test outcomes were compared using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), adjusting for the corresponding baseline score, previous AI training experience, frequency of AI use, and digital literacy. Results In the intervention group, AI literacy increased significantly from 55.67 ± 9.84 to 65.01 ± 8.81 ( P < 0.001), as did attitudes toward AI, which increased from 48.07 ± 6.77 to 51.72 ± 9.90 ( P = 0.049). Neither outcome changed significantly in the control group. After adjustment for covariates, the intervention group had significantly higher post-test scores for AI literacy (adjusted mean difference = 11.01, 95% CI 8.55–13.47; P < 0.001) and attitudes toward AI (adjusted mean difference = 4.60, 95% CI 1.98–7.21; P < 0.001). Autonomous learning competency changed little in the intervention group ( P = 0.578) but declined significantly in the control group ( P < 0.001). The adjusted post-test difference also favored the intervention group (adjusted mean difference = 10.94, 95% CI 7.44–14.43; P < 0.001). Conclusions AI/GenAI-assisted blended teaching was associated with higher AI literacy and more favorable attitudes toward AI, while autonomous learning competency remained relatively stable in the intervention group but declined in the control group. Structured AI education integrating conceptual learning, practical application, and responsible AI use may be a valuable addition to undergraduate nursing education.

items.title: Applying artificial intelligence to support cardiovascular risk prediction in resource-constrained settings: qualitative insights from Indonesian doctors
items.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk assessment underpins preventive care. Although machine learning models often outperform traditional risk prediction methods, adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)-based clinical decision support (CDS) tools remains limited, especially in resource-constrained settings. This study explored the sociotechnical context of CVD risk assessment in resource-constrained settings and identified potential applications for AI-based CDS. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 27 Indonesian doctors, including general practitioners and cardiologists. Interviews examined clinical decision-making processes, challenges associated with resource constraints, and potential use cases for AI-based CDS. Data were analyzed using a deductive thematic approach informed by the SEIPS (Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety) framework. Doctors reported managing high patient volumes, relying on paper-based medical records, and making largely subjective decisions due to limited access to confirmatory investigations and specialist support. Acute coronary syndrome resulting from atherosclerosis was identified as the most common and important clinical problem. Participants highlighted atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk assessment as a promising application for AI-based CDS because it uses widely available clinical information and can support preventive care decisions. Implementation of AI-based CDS should be guided by local clinical needs and sociotechnical context. Further research is needed to evaluate effects on clinical decision-making and patient outcomes.

items.title: Artificial intelligence anxiety and literacy among higher vocational nursing students: the mediating role of artificial intelligence self-efficacy in a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Abstract Background As AI becomes integrated into nursing education and clinical practice, students must develop the competence to use, evaluate, and ethically govern AI-generated information. However, the psychological mechanisms linking students’ emotional responses to AI and their AI literacy remain underexplored in vocational nursing contexts. This study aimed to examine the mediating role of artificial intelligence (AI) self-efficacy in the relationship between AI anxiety and AI literacy among higher vocational nursing students. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted using a convenience sample of 921 nursing students from five higher vocational colleges in Sichuan, China. Participants completed the Chinese Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale, the revised Chinese Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale, and the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale. Structural equation modeling was used to test the mediating hypothesis. Results AI anxiety was negatively correlated with AI self-efficacy (r = − 0.470) and AI literacy (r = − 0.370), while AI self-efficacy was positively correlated with AI literacy (r = 0.392). AI self-efficacy partially mediated the association between AI anxiety and AI literacy, accounting for 42.22% of the total effect (indirect effect β = −0.171, 95% BC CI [− 0.255, − 0.100]). After adjustment for covariates, attitude toward nursing and residence remained independently associated with AI literacy. Conclusions AI literacy among higher vocational nursing students is shaped by psychological (AI anxiety, AI self-efficacy), professional (attitude toward nursing), and educational (residence) factors. AI education should be embedded in competency-based nursing preparation with emphasis on critical evaluation, safe application, professional accountability, and equitable access to structured learning opportunities.

items.title: Artificial intelligence meets LCA: a critical analysis from technical, ethical, and organizational perspectives
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) holds strong potential to automate repetitive and data-intensive life cycle assessment (LCA) tasks, thereby reducing costs, enabling scalability, and improving data access. This study critically analyses the integration of AI into LCA from technical, ethical, and organizational perspectives. It aims to evaluate how AI can be implemented across LCA workflow steps to enhance efficiency without compromising effectiveness, inclusivity, and core LCA ethical values such as transparency and scientific integrity. Methods We conducted literature review to identify and characterise the technical approaches of current AI-LCA applications across academic research and commercial tools, complemented by a survey assessing current AI uptake in LCA practice and perceived ethical risks. Ethical risks, like accountability or fairness, were derived from existing AI ethical principles and analysed for their potential conflict with LCA ethical values. Organizational implications including changes in work practices and regional disparities were explored, with attention to role of AI in social LCA. Identified applications were critically assessed against four categories: technical maturity, potential to enhance LCA practices, operational feasibility, and ethical risks, and used to qualitatively derive criticality of ethical risks. Results and discussion Most AI-LCA applications focus on predicting impact scores and estimating missing inventory data. Few are employing generative AI, while it is mainly used by practitioners for auxiliary tasks like literature review and report writing. Despite high automation potential, most applications remain at proof-of-concept stage, lack end-to-end workflow integration, and face operational barriers for inclusivity (coding skills, restricted access) resulting in low adoption. Most critical ethical risks relate to fairness, transparency, accountability and sustainability, driven by black-box models, poor documentation, and representation bias, and threaten all core LCA values. Emerging commercial AI-LCA tools present a high potential to widen AI adoption in LCA, but present higher risks toward sustainability, transparency, safety and security. AI is expected to shift LCA stakeholders’ roles from manual tasks to supervising algorithms and validating outputs, while potentially reinforcing regional disparities due to unequal access to AI tools, data, and expertise. Conclusion AI can significantly enhance LCA efficiency and scalability, but without robust collaborative governance it may undermine methodological rigor and ethical principles. Responsible integration requires need-based adoption, standardized protocols for evaluating AI models in LCA context, human-in-the-loop validation for value choices, transparent documentation, and proactive attention to fairness and inclusivity. These findings provide a foundation for guidance toward effective, inclusive, and responsible use of AI in LCA.

items.title: AutoRSE: Evaluating LLM Agents as Recommendation Engineers for Self-Evolving Recommender Systems
items.abstract: Recommender Systems Engineer Agents (RSE-Agents), which use LLM-based agents to autonomously improve recommendation algorithms, are emerging as a promising paradigm. However, their capabilities and limitations remain poorly understood due to the lack of a unified, standardized evaluation framework and systematic trajectory-level analysis. To address this gap, we introduce AutoRSE, an evaluation framework spanning six representative industrial-grade recommendation tasks, and conduct a large-scale empirical study of three frontier LLMs across three widely used agent harnesses. Our results show that RSE-Agents consistently enhance the performance of backbones on five of the six tasks, with an average relative improvement of 16.1%, indicating that they can already autonomously improve recommendation performance. However, trajectory-level analysis also reveals that current RSE-Agents function primarily as engineering optimizers rather than algorithmic improvers: their gains are largely driven by hyperparameter tuning, training strategies, and model ensembling, while genuine algorithmic innovations are rare. Since the largest gains in recommender systems often stem from algorithmic advances, this behavior underscores a fundamental limitation of current RSE-Agents. To probe this limitation, we perform idea-injection experiments and show that agents equipped with innovative ideas from frontier research or human experts achieve substantially larger improvements than those relying on self-generated ideas. These results suggest that idea generation is a central bottleneck of current RSE-Agents, highlights a key direction for the future recommendation system research. Our implementation is publicly available on GitHub: https://github.com/Ray-Tiann/AutoRSE.

items.title: Balancing Cultural Preservation and Design: A Study on the Generative Artificial Intelligence-Empowered Framework for the Sustainable Design of Intangible Cultural Heritage
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) is a form of AI technology that can automatically generate new content, such as text, images, and audio, based on prompts. This study explores the opportunities and structural challenges of using Gen-AI to promote sustainable design in the field of intangible cultural heritage (ICH) from the perspectives of ICH designers and relevant experts. The research employed a variety of methods, including interviews (n= 40), grounded theory, the Delphi method (n = 20), exploratory factor analysis (n = 312), confirmatory factor analysis (n = 324), and expert interviews (n = 10). The study evaluated deep-seated issues arising from Gen-AI’s intervention in ICH design practices, such as cultural subjectivity, knowledge, power relations, and value circulation, through the lenses of Cultural Ecology, Extraction of Intangible Cultural Heritage Genes, Sustainable Communication, Technology Generation, and Human–Machine Collaborative Design. The results suggest that Gen-AI’s empowerment involves a tension between technological generative capabilities and cultural accuracy, as well as systemic-level transformations such as balancing communication efficiency with cultural depth and human–machine collaboration, and re-configuring the designer’s role.

items.title: Between tradition and algorithm: Human–AI co-creation in textile design education and its implications for cultural authenticity
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid integration of generative AI into creative industries has intensified debates about the future of culturally grounded design practice. This study examines how three production conditions (human-only, AI-assisted, and fully autonomous AI) differentially affect the perceived cultural fidelity, creativity, aesthetics, and commercial viability of textile designs rooted in traditional Anatolian kilim motifs, a question with limited prior empirical evidence in design education. Using a within-subjects design, fifteen undergraduate textile design students produced designs under each condition, using a generative AI platform with substantial commercial reach in the Turkish textile sector for the AI-involved conditions. A panel of ten expert evaluators, five academics and five industry designers, rated 45 designs against a seven-criterion rubric under blind conditions. Cultural fidelity, creativity, originality, and aesthetics differed significantly across conditions (all p < .05). Both human-only and AI-assisted designs preserved cultural fidelity at equivalent levels, and both significantly exceeded fully autonomous AI outputs. Paradoxically, fully autonomous AI outputs received the highest scores for creativity and originality, pointing to a trade-off between perceived novelty and cultural coherence. No significant differences emerged for commercial viability, technical feasibility, or compositional integrity, indicating parity across production methods on industrially relevant dimensions. Academic and industry evaluators converged on cultural fidelity judgements while diverging on more subjective aesthetic criteria. These findings suggest that human involvement acts as a cultural filter that cannot be replicated through textual instruction alone, and that even minimal human intervention, selecting and lightly editing AI-generated variants, is sufficient to preserve culturally identifiable design characteristics. The results have implications for textile design pedagogy, for AI governance in heritage-sensitive industries, and for theorising human–AI co-creation in cultural production contexts.

items.title: Capability-Adaptive Intelligent Assistance in Industry 5.0 Manufacturing: A Systematic Review and Research Framework
items.abstract: Abstract Industry 5.0 reframes manufacturing around human-centricity, sustainability, and resilience, and a growing literature has developed intelligent assistance systems human-robot collaboration, AI-driven perception, digital twins, and extended-reality interfaces in pursuit of this aim. Whether this literature accommodates the heterogeneity of the workers it aims to center has not been systematically established. This review analyzes 14,346 Web of Science records (2016–2026, screened from 15,038 raw records across 19 export files, using an empirically validated Advanced Search query) addressing Industry 5.0 manufacturing. Bibliometric analysis confirms a technology-dominant field: robotics/cobots and AI/ML content appear in 51.9% and 26.8% of records respectively, while human-factors and interaction-modality content appear in 11.6% and 10.0%. A purposively verified subsample of 62 records 19 disability-explicit, 8 age-explicit, 4 cognitive/neurodiversity-explicit, and 31 addressing digital literacy or general capability accommodation was identified and hand-checked against the full corpus; despite this real and previously undercounted body of work, capability-diversity terms remain essentially absent from the field's dominant keyword co-occurrence structure (fewer than 3 co-occurrences for any disability-related pair, against 425 for the corpus's leading pair). This indicates a literature that exists but has not been synthesized, is rarely cross-cited, and remains disconnected from the mainstream human-centric Industry 5.0 discourse and its dominant AI-driven technology stack. We propose the Capability-Adaptive Intelligent Assistance Framework for Industry 5.0 (CAIA-5.0), connecting this scattered capability-accommodation literature to current AI-driven assistance mechanisms, with one extension profile-conditioned autonomy allocation explicitly flagged as untested. A six-item research agenda specifies the empirical, technological, and synthesis work required to connect this fragmented literature into a coherent, industrially applicable framework. The review offers manufacturing system designers, human-factors engineers, and policymakers a diagnostic basis and implementation roadmap for inclusive intelligent assistance.

items.title: Changes in Perceptions of Trust in Human-AI Interactions
items.abstract: This study examined how educational briefings about Artificial Intelligence (AI) hallucinations influence user trust, caution, and willingness to continue using AI systems. We recruited 51 participants through the online platform Prolific for an online questionnaire evaluating AI use and task-focused AI scenarios. After questions about trust and AI, participants read about common inaccuracies in Large Language Models. Participants showed a significant decrease in self-reported trust, indicating increased awareness of AI limitations. Contrary to expectations, perceptions of AI reliability and competence did not predict willingness to reuse AI in academic scenarios. Affective trust played a stronger role than cognitive trust, with perceived emotional support significantly predicting forgiveness of AI errors. Increased caution also predicted greater recalibration of trust, although willingness to continue using AI remained high. These findings suggest that educational interventions can promote calibrated trust in AI without discouraging continued use, highlighting the importance of transparency and context-sensitive design.

items.title: Closed-loop cognitive state control: a hypothesis framework for real-time estimation, stabilization, and recovery of task-specific high-performance cognitive states
items.abstract: Human performance often fails not because latent capacity is absent, but because access to high-functioning cognitive states is unstable under fatigue, distraction, overload, and pressure. This hypothesis paper proposes closed-loop cognitive state control—informally, supercognition —as a neuroengineering objective: rapid entry into, stabilization of, and recovery of an individual's highest available task-specific cognitive state. The framework treats cognition as a partially observable dynamical system whose latent states would be inferred from multimodal behavioral, physiological, contextual, and neural signals, and specifies a five-layer architecture comprising multimodal sensing, latent-state inference, predictive transition modeling, closed-loop intervention, and a longitudinal personal neural twin. The proposal is situated against existing closed-loop and neuroadaptive architectures, with an explicit statement of what is and is not new. The state ontology is given as a set of falsifiable assumptions rather than an intuitive taxonomy. Candidate computational implementations are specified for each layer, including hidden semi-Markov and switching state-space models, Bayesian and Kalman filtering, sequence models, hazard models, contextual bandits, model-predictive control, and offline reinforcement learning. The personal neural twin receives an operational specification covering its data requirements, update schedule, calibration and drift-monitoring criteria, and failure modes. Predictive and causal claims are separated, with the evidentiary requirements stated for each. The paper engages directly with the literature that challenges the framework's feasibility, including biomarker reliability, mixed neurofeedback findings, cross-task and cross-subject generalization failure, and the ecological-validity gap in wearable neurotechnology. Operational definitions, application scenarios, a validation protocol with power and diversity requirements, an expanded ethics and governance analysis, and a staged research roadmap are provided. No component of the architecture has been implemented or evaluated here: no simulation, clinical trial, or empirical efficacy claim is presented, and the validation programme described is prospective. The contribution is a falsifiable systems-engineering hypothesis for cognitive-state control.

items.title: CogArena: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents on Interactive Behavioral Experiments
items.abstract: Claims about the cognitive capabilities of large language models are typically tested by translating behavioral paradigms into text prompts, bypassing the visual interfaces and time pressure through which human participants actually engage with experiments. At the same time, AI agents can now complete online behavioral tasks and produce human-like data, which raises concerns that online datasets in the social and behavioral sciences are increasingly open to contamination. We introduce CogArena, a benchmark of ten experimental paradigms from the social and behavioral sciences. Agents complete the experiments through a standard web browser, working with the same visual stimuli and response interfaces that online participants use. A three-level scoring procedure evaluates whether the agent completed the task, how accurately it performed, and whether its data show the behavioral signatures each paradigm reliably produces in people. Across four multimodal models, each run ten times per task, we find that finishing an experiment and reproducing its signatures are different things. Many sessions did not finish, and those that did reproduced some signatures reliably and others not at all. CogArena provides the tasks, scoring code, and a public leaderboard for new submissions.

items.title: CoHARL: Co-Evolving Agent Policies and Executable Harnesses with Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents interact with their environments through executable harnesses that govern tool use and feedback. Optimizing a harness for a fixed policy overlooks how its behavior changes during learning, while training a policy under a fixed harness leaves the interface that generates its training experience unchanged. This motivates adapting the harness throughout policy training. We introduce CoHARL, a population-based reinforcement learning framework that co-evolves a shared policy and a population of executable harnesses. The policy learns from rollouts across the population, and a proposer uses its execution traces to revise harness code during training. CoHARL achieves a 27.6% mean resolved rate on SWE-rebench, improving over harness-only search by 6.4 percentage points. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 show gains in software engineering and terminal-based tasks. Under matched training budgets, CoHARL also outperforms searching for a harness once before RL and alternating policy updates with revisions to a single active harness.

items.title: Competence narrowing in AI-assisted oral English instruction: A quasi-experimental study of the spiral synergy framework
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative AI tools into spoken English instruction has produced measurable fluency and accuracy gains, but whether these are evenly distributed across the dimensions of communicative competence remains underexplored. This quasi-experimental study compares the Spiral Synergy Framework (SSF), a three-layer pedagogical sequence (AI Consolidation, Bridging Tasks, Interpersonal Activation), against conventional AI-integrated instruction in two intact Business English classes at a Chinese higher vocational college (experimental n = 36, control n = 34), using oral recordings at three time points scored on five competence dimensions, 15 weeks of classroom observation, and an intra-rater reliability check. The two classes differed significantly at baseline on the oral composite score and three of five dimensions (control higher), though not on CET-4 proficiency or questionnaire items. Because treatment is confounded with class membership and both classes received AI-assisted practice, findings are reported as associations rather than demonstrated causal effects. Linear mixed-effects models testing Group × Time interactions across five outcomes (four dimensions and the composite), corrected for multiple comparisons, identified one outcome - real-time responsiveness - on which the classes diverged: the experimental class maintained responsiveness across the semester while the control class declined despite its baseline advantage (Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted p = .029), a result that held under a cluster-robust sensitivity check. No corrected between-group difference was found for improvisation, coherence, naturalness, or the composite score; improvisation declined descriptively in both classes over the semester. Classroom observation data (experimental class only) document a recurring, non-monotonic cycle of AI-dependency reduction and rebound across 15 weeks. Intra-rater test-retest reliability of the oral-competence ratings was moderate to good (ICC = .67-.91), though this reflects a single rater familiar with participants rather than independent inter-rater agreement. Implications for multidimensional assessment, task sequencing, and cautious interpretation of AI-integrated curriculum research are discussed.

items.title: Conditional Values: The Contingent Foundations of Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: How do broader values shape whether people judge artificial intelligence (AI) as good or bad for humanity? This article analyzes provisional World Values Survey Wave 8 data from 40,960 respondents in 24 country samples using pooled and national prediction models, outcome-independent respondent profiles, and groups of countries. The analysis reveals a cross-country anchor: general optimism about science and technology is the strongest pooled predictor of favorable AI evaluation and recurs among the leading predictors in every national sample. Expert authority, education and information access, selected forms of trust, openness, and demographic position provide nationally distinctive patterns. Eleven value profiles formed without AI attitudes span 49.1% to 62.2% favorable evaluation. Most evaluative variation occurs within these profiles, making them useful contexts for identifying how the same values distinguish favorable from unfavorable evaluators in different social configurations. Institutional legitimacy, structural advantage, information connectedness, personal choice, redistribution, and openness differentiate evaluations in particular profiles. The same axis can relate differently to AI evaluation across profiles: secular reasoning has a significant positive association among secular moderate pluralists but a suggestive negative association among institution-trusting civic joiners. Together, the findings show that public receptivity to AI as technological change has a common predictive anchor but develops within plural configurations of resources, institutions, authority, openness, and social position. This distinction helps anticipate where generalized technological optimism is likely to travel and where AI deployment and governance will encounter context-specific sources of legitimacy or concern.

items.title: Correction or Manipulation? Measuring Epistemic Vigilance in LLM Agents Under User Pressure
items.abstract: LLM agents that answer questions and act on behalf of users must decide when to yield to a user who disagrees. Disagreement may correct a genuine error or may be an attempt at manipulation. Prior work shows that models frequently abandon correct answers when challenged by users, yet it remains unclear whether they distinguish correction from manipulation or merely differ in their propensity to concede. We examine this question across seven LLMs from four vendors in two studies, one on the answers agents give and one on the actions they take as customer-support agents whose policy permits account changes only for verified users. Simulated users push toward correct and incorrect answers with graded pressure. Following research on epistemic vigilance, the pressure either appeals to the source, such as claimed authority, or offers content the agent cannot verify, namely a cited source. Drawing on signal detection theory, we measure on a set of benchmark questions how much more readily each agent concedes to correction than to manipulation, separately from its overall propensity to concede. Citations made five of seven models readier to concede and four worse at discriminating, while stronger wording added little. In the agentic study, five models never violated the verification policy, including models that readily abandoned correct answers, so concession on answers did not predict violations of policy. Ministral 3B violated the policy mainly under claimed authority, and Ministral 8B reported changes it had not made. An instruction to revise only on verifiable evidence chiefly shifted propensity to concede rather than improving discrimination. Concession rates alone are therefore misleading, and agents should be evaluated on both their discrimination and the actions they take.

items.title: Detailed Balance in Large-Language-Model-Driven Agents
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-driven agents are emerging as a powerful new paradigm for solving complex problems. Despite the empirical success of these practices, a theoretical framework to understand and unify their macroscopic dynamics remains lacking. This paper proposes a method based on the least action principle to estimate the underlying generative directionality of LLMs embedded within agents. By experimentally measuring the transition probabilities between LLM-generated states, we report evidence consistent with a tendency toward detailed balance in LLM-generated transitions, indicating that LLM generation may not be achieved by generally learning rule sets and strategies, but rather by implicitly learning a class of underlying potential functions that may transcend different LLM architectures and prompt templates. To our knowledge, this provides an effective macroscopic description of LLM generative dynamics that does not depend on specific model details. This work is an attempt to establish a macroscopic dynamics theory of complex AI systems, aiming to elevate the study of AI agents from a collection of engineering practices to a science built on effective measurements that are predictable and quantifiable.

items.title: Developing a Remote Operations Center for Uncrewed and Autonomously-Capable Maritime Surface Ships
items.abstract: Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS) are increasingly enabled by advances in automation, autonomy, network connectivity and shoreside support systems. These technologies create opportunities to offload tasks to Remote Operating Centers (ROCs), reduce and/or remove onboard crew, thus facilitating a wide variety of approaches for how ships are controlled and monitored in comparison to traditional shipping. This paper details a design case study of an ROC for an 8-meter diesel-electric uncrewed and autonomous-capable test ship operating in North Atlantic Canadian waters. A series of user-centered workshops and design iterations were implemented to redesign and refine the ROC physical work environment and Human-Machine Interfaces to better align with the goals and demands of shoreside operators. This work provides methodological and design contributions to MASS ROC development, while also creating a foundation for human-performance testing involving ROC operators and autonomous surface ships for the next phases of research and development.

items.abstract: Prior research suggests that vehicles with longer-wavelength or lighter colors are associated with faster perceived speeds compared to shorter-wavelength or darker colors, but TTC estimates were not measured. In the current study, participants viewed a simulated traffic scene in which a red or blue vehicle approached for 3 s and disappeared. Participants pressed a button when they believed the vehicle would reach their position. Red vehicles were judged to arrive sooner (TTC was underestimated) than blue vehicles (TTC was overestimated), but only when TTC was 4 s. Results suggest that vehicle color may be used as a heuristic cue to judge TTC when cognitive motion extrapolation demands are putatively higher.

items.title: Drivers and academic outcomes of generative AI use among university students in Benin
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being integrated into higher education, offering potential gains in efficiency and quality, yet there are concerns about its cognitive and behavioral consequences. This study surveyed 633 university students in Benin to examine factors associated with GenAI use and its academic, behavioral and psychological outcomes. Drawing on the Expectancy Value Theory and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), we used Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling to assess how Academic Workload, Time Pressure, and motivational sensitivities relate to GenAI use and its association with Academic Performance, Procrastination, and Self-Perceived Memory Decline. Results show that Academic Workload, Time Pressure, and motivational factors (Sensitivity to Rewards and Quality) were positively associated with GenAI use, which was widespread – more than 90% of students reporting use at least twice per week. GenAI use was positively associated with higher Academic Performance, but also with increased Procrastination and Self-Perceived Memory Decline. Contrary to prior research, age, gender, and education level were not significantly associated with GenAI use, reflecting the widespread GenAI adoption across student groups. These findings highlight GenAI’s dual role as both a potential performance-support tool and a mechanism of cognitive offloading, underscoring the need for balanced integration strategies that leverage AI-assisted efficiency while preserving meaningful cognitive engagement and mitigating risks associated with overreliance on AI tools.

items.title: Driving Innovative Work Behaviour Among Professors: The Mediating Role of Work Engagement in Malaysian Private Universities
items.abstract: Innovation is increasingly important for organisations seeking to adapt to rapid economic changes and sustain competitiveness through effective human capital utilisation and employee creativity. In Malaysia, strengthening innovation outcomes aligns with the national aspiration to develop a knowledge and innovation-driven economy, as reflected in the Thirteenth Malaysia Plan (RMK13) 2026–2030. As key academic knowledge professionals, professors play an important role in knowledge creation, research and institutional innovation. However, empirical understanding of the personal resources and work-related mechanisms that foster innovative work behaviour (IWB) among professors in Malaysian private universities remains limited. Guided by Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) and Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) Theory, this study examines the relationships of self-efficacy (SE) and intrinsic motivation (IM) with IWB and evaluates the mediating role of work engagement (WE). Using a quantitative research design and purposive sampling, data were collected from 205 professors across private universities in Malaysia and analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) via SmartPLS 4. The findings show that WE is positively and significantly associated with IWB. SE and IM are positively and significantly associated with WE and WE significantly mediates the relationships of both SE and IM with IWB. The findings contribute to Strategic Human Resource Management (SHRM) literature by highlighting WE as an important mechanism linking personal resources with IWB in the Malaysian higher education sector. Practically, the study provides insights for HR practitioners and institutional leaders to strengthen personal resources and work engagement, optimise talent management, and foster supportive workplace environments that promote academic innovation.

items.title: Edhivo: An AI-Native Platform for Scalable Assessment and Instant Feedback in Higher Education
items.abstract: Scaling assessment in higher education faces two intertwined bottlenecks: the cognitive burden of authoring assessments and the inability to semantically evaluate open-ended responses, which together create a persistent feedback gap that hinders student learning outcomes. To address these challenges, we present Edhivo, an AI-native pedagogical platform that addresses both bottlenecks through a vertically integrated system for content delivery, assessment, and reporting. Edhivo employs a Dual-LLM pipeline: one model generates context-aware assessments for both multiple-choice and open-ended questions, from instructor-provided materials, while a second model performs multi-criteria, rubric-based evaluation of student responses, enabling near-instant qualitative feedback at multiple hierarchical levels. All AI interactions are source-grounded to reduce hallucination risk, and a Human-in-the-Loop review process preserves instructor authority. We demonstrate Edhivo's efficacy through a pilot deployment at Stony Brook University in a real classroom environment in 2026 spring, where it supports high-frequency assessment creation and evaluation for a cohort of 36 students throughout a full semester, significantly reducing authoring effort and feedback latency while enabling novel pedagogical designs centered on active learning.

items.title: Effects of multi-attributional diversity for targets and perceivers of stereotypes in computer-supported collaborative learning
items.abstract: Higher distance education opens a wide range of opportunities for students with different socio-demographic backgrounds (e.g., age, gender, native language) and task-related skills (e.g., experience in scientific reading or online learning, previous degrees). Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL), where students work together in virtual groups, is a common teaching method in distance education. The current research investigates the consequences of stereotypes for targets and perceivers during the formation and collaboration phases in multi-attributionally diverse CSCL groups by systematically examining the individual level and the CSCL-group level. N = 2,023 students in 285 CSCL groups participated in a longitudinal field study in the introductory module of the BSc Psychology curriculum at a large European public distance teaching university. Analyses of multilevel models corresponding to pre-registered hypotheses replicated the findings of previous research that CSCL groups with high socio-demographic and high task-related diversity showed lower structural integration during collaboration. To explain this at-risk constellation for CSCL groups with highly diverse members, we investigated the role of being a target vs. perceiver of negative stereotypes within the group. Targets experiencing social identity threat reported a lower sense of belonging to the CSCL group and, consequently, lower motivation to initiate and maintain social relations with other group members. Moreover, targets generally reported higher social identity threat. Findings are discussed in terms of social-psychological approaches to microdynamics in CSCL groups and interventions to mitigate effects of diversity and stereotyping in higher distance education.

items.title: Engagement Profiles in AI-Assisted ESAP: Associations with AI Use Indicators and Speaking Performance
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) offers opportunities for repeated practice and feedback in English language learning. However, how students participate in these learning activities requires further investigation. This study examined learning engagement profiles and their associations with GenAI use and speaking performance among 500 STEM master’s students in an AI-assisted ESAP speaking course at a Chinese university. Latent profile analysis used self-reported behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement scores collected in Week 15. Separate R3STEP models examined associations with self-reported weekly GenAI use frequency and average weekly online duration. BCH analyses compared posttest speaking performance across profiles while adjusting for pretest scores. Four profiles emerged: Low Engagement Profile (P1, 22.4%), High Engagement Profile (P2, 38.2%), Low Emotional Engagement Profile (P3, 24.0%), and Low Cognitive Engagement Profile (P4, 15.4%). Proportions were based on most likely assignments. After Holm correction, longer online duration was associated with higher odds of membership in P2, P3, and P4 relative to P1. More frequent GenAI use was associated with membership in P2 and P4 relative to P3. P2 had significantly higher baseline-adjusted overall speaking scores than all other profiles. These findings provide person-centered evidence of learner heterogeneity in AI-assisted ESAP. They highlight the value of considering multidimensional engagement configurations alongside GenAI use indicators when interpreting differences in speaking performance.
