items.title: From Design Principles to Practice: Validation of a UX Design Checklist for Affective Conversational Agents in Mental Well-Being
items.abstract: University students' psychological well-being is a critical public health concern, creating demand for digital interventions that are both safe and effective. Although conversational agents offer scalable support, existing usability heuristics cannot address complex affective dimensions such as emotional containment and clinical safety, revealing a gap in specialized design frameworks. To address this, the study introduces the “Affective Design Checklist,” a practical inspection tool for developing and auditing mental health conversational agents. Using Jabareen's conceptual framework analysis with a PRISMA-guided systematic review of 43 key articles, the instrument underwent a two-stage validation by a panel of ten experts, achieving a scale-level Content Validity Index (S-CVI/Ave) of 0.971, with near-unanimous agreement on ethical and regulatory dimensions. This research translates abstract bioethical and affective computing principles into actionable verification items, offering a specialized standard to ensure digital interventions are technically usable, affectively competent, and ethically aligned with student needs.

items.title: From digital access to workforce capability: a comparative documentary study of AI-relevant learning ecosystems in Singapore, Europe and India
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence is typically linked to the learning platform, the diagnosis of skills and employment services, but the advantages of AI to workforce training are still not even as the skills acquired in the learning platform are not automatically available for use. There is already a significant amount of published work that discusses automation risk, as well as digital competencies and the role of AI in learning and development, but less comparative focus on the institutions that transform learning resources into recognised skills and employability through the operation and use of AI enabled and/or AI relevant learning environments. By designing it around the theoretically motivated Capability Approach of Sen, this study analyzed SkillsFuture Singapore and the European Digital Skills and Jobs Coalition and India’s National Career Service using a qualitative comparative documentary approach. Thematic analysis was performed using secondary data such as all documents of platforms, official documents, intergovernmental document and peer-reviewed literature, which were publicly available and interpreted each case one by one as a documentary thematic analysis. It suggests that the strength of workforce-learning ecosystems emerges when combined with trying to make digital accessible, within an affordable context, with digital skills, counselling, assisted access, language-sensitive design, recognition by employers, transparency in governance, and evidence of outcomes. With Singapore demonstrating coordinated lifelong learning, Europe demonstrates the good and bad of mobilising digital skills across multiple stakeholders and levels and India helps to show how to apply the reach of platforms to employment-related skills inclusion at large scale. The analysis of the study presents a framework for capability conversion, which attempts to simultaneously analyze the AI-relevant workforce's learning, even though the mere presence of the platform does not guarantee it is effective. The shocks are not "user" shocks or "platform-internal" shocks because of the documentary nature of the evidence, which leaves room for analytical interpretations of the findings as more representative of outcomes in the labour market rather than causal interpretations.

items.title: From orchestra to classroom: learner-centered music training as a tool to support motivation to learn
items.abstract: Fostering more self-determined forms of motivation in students remains a key challenge in education. According to self-determination theory (SDT), educational environments supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness enhance more autonomous forms of motivation. Music education in collaborative, learner-centered formats may provide such conditions. This study investigates whether participation in learner-centered orchestral training is associated with changes in children's general academic motivation.The study involved 113 children aged 8–10 years. Half joined a three-month orchestral program emphasizing active participation, peer collaboration, and public performance. The other half formed a control group with no music training. Motivation was assessed pre- and post-training using the Academic Self-Regulation Questionnaire.Children in the music group showed a greater reduction in external regulation compared to the control group. For intrinsic motivation, a descriptive trend toward improvement was observed in the music group relative to the control group, although the Group x Time interaction did not reach statistical significance.These findings suggest that learner-centered orchestral training may support a shift towards more self-determined forms of motivation, primarily through reduced external regulation.

items.title: From Proposal to Discovery: Attribution, Validation, and Responsibility in Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Science / De la propuesta al descubrimiento: atribución, validación y responsabilidad en la ciencia asistida por inteligencia artificial
items.abstract: ENGLISH This critical conceptual essay examines how to distinguish a proposed AI-assisted scientific discovery from its validation, the documented contributions of participants, and responsibility for communicating the result. It develops a four-register framework covering the scientific claim, the standard of evidence attained, the provenance of contributions, and communication responsibility. Published examples illustrate why generating hypotheses or computational results is not, by itself, equivalent to validating all claims made about them. The essay reports no original experiment or systematic review; the proposed framework has not been empirically validated. This record contains the complete English and Spanish editions, Version 1.0. Desarrolla un marco de cuatro registros: afirmación científica, estándar de prueba alcanzado, procedencia de las contribuciones y responsabilidad comunicativa. items.abstract: This reflective article critically examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents configured as educational tutors in secondary education. Based on a rigorous review of meta-analyses, international case studies, and specialized academic literature, it explores the conceptual foundations of intelligent tutoring and contemporary models of digital pedagogy. It examines real-world applications of intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), their benefits in terms of learning personalization, immediate feedback, student autonomy, and intrinsic motivation. Likewise, ethical challenges such as algorithmic bias, risks of dehumanizing educational processes, and vulnerabilities related to data privacy are identified. Finally, pedagogical guidelines are presented for the ethical and effective integration of AI agents in school settings, emphasizing teacher training, student-centered design, and continuous educational impact assessment.

items.title: GARDEN: Generalist Autonomous Reward Design Through Evidence Navigation for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables teams of agents, such as robots and autonomous vehicles, to learn coordinated behavior, but what such teams learn is largely determined by their reward function. Because task success alone provides too little guidance for learning, intermediate rewards are usually designed by hand, and this effort must often be repeated whenever the environment or the team changes. Large language models (LLMs) can automate the effort by writing reward functions as code, yet the resulting rewards are typically designed and tested in a single setting. To enable their reuse across settings, GARDEN (Generalist Autonomous Reward Design through Evidence Navigation) is proposed, in which one reward program is developed for a family of related scenarios and transferred, unchanged, to scenarios that were not available during its design. During development, environment code, training records, and agent behavior are investigated by an LLM reward engineer, and draft rewards are tested in trial training runs, while the learning algorithm and the rule for selecting the final reward are held fixed. On unseen scenarios of the Overcooked and SMAX benchmarks, task returns were increased by 58.2% and 52.5% over the default rewards on two kitchen layouts, and the mean win rate in two combat scenarios was raised from 51.0% to 89.9%. Under matched candidate and probe budgets, this exceeded the 84.2% and 79.2% obtained with fixed diagnostic feedback and Eureka-inspired reward reflection. These results show that a single autonomously engineered reward can be reused effectively across related cooperative scenarios.

items.title: GEPA-Curator: Curated Learning for Self Improving Agents
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in multi-turn agentic workloads that require sustained interaction with complex environments. Existing reflective prompt optimizers such as GEPA learn from failed rollouts, but agentic failures can also come from prompt weaknesses, harness limitations, stochastic execution, or noisy judges. We argue that such failures may not provide useful learning signal, and may even be harmful; and thus it is essential to curate which tasks are provided to the prompt optimizer for better performance. We introduce GEPA-Curator, a framework that augments the prompt optimizer to select which agent experiences should shape prompt optimization. In particular, GEPA-Curator consists of two components: task curation, which filters out tasks that are likely to provide noisy or unreliable learning signals, and prior success retrieval, which selectively retrieves past successful trajectories for a task and provides them as additional context to the prompt optimizer. We evaluate GEPA-Curator on GoBrowse, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and $τ$-bench, using both Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 5 as optimizer models. GEPA-Curator matches or exceeds the mean performance of both baselines, with gains of up to 20.7% over GEPA and 21.2% over ACE.

items.title: Governing AI Coding Agents: An Empirical Analysis of Repository Artifacts
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose: Software projects are increasingly using repository-level governance artifacts, such as \texttt{CLAUDE.md} and \texttt{AGENTS.md}, to communicate project-specific guidance to AI coding agents. Although these artifacts have become an important mechanism for governing AI coding agents, little is known about the governance practices and liabilities they encode, or whether their observable characteristics are consistent with organizational governance capability. Method: To examine these questions, we conducted an exploratory sequential mixed-methods study of 555 AI agent governance artifacts collected from public GitHub repositories. Using Socio-Technical Grounded Theory for Data Analysis (STGT4DA), we developed taxonomies of governance practices and governance liabilities, which were converted into a structured codebook for LLM-based classification. The codebook was evaluated against manually coded reference labels and applied to the corpus to examine whether these artifacts exhibit observable characteristics theoretically associated with organizational governance capability. Results: The findings reveal that these artifacts primarily emphasize knowledge transfer, process guidance, and coding standards, whereas explicit oversight mechanisms, such as human approval gates, remain comparatively limited. The analysis also identifies recurring governance liabilities, most commonly vague instructions (36%) and fragmentation debt (35%). We found no systematic association between the governance observed in the artifacts and the repository maturity indicators examined in this study, nor did governance vary systematically across the application domains examined as broad proxies for potential operational consequences. The artifacts also showed limited evidence of characteristics associated with institutionalized governance, particularly regarding accountability mechanisms, coherence between governance content and governance quality, and project-specific adaptation. Conclusion: This study provides an empirical investigation of repository-level AI agent governance from an organizational capability perspective. By examining governance artifacts according to the governance functions they perform rather than solely the information they contain, the study develops taxonomies of governance practices and liabilities and an evaluated LLM-based classification approach for systematically characterizing AI agent governance in research and practice.

items.title: Human-AI Collaboration in Language Assessment: EFL Learners' Trust, Anxiety, and AI Literacy in AI-Mediated Writing Feedback
items.abstract: This study aimed to examine how EFL learners' trust in AI feedback, AI-related anxiety, and AI literacy relate to their engagement with, and uptake of, AI-mediated written corrective feedback. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design combined survey data from 300 university EFL learners, analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), with follow-up semi-structured interviews (n = 16); the structural model explained 48% of the variance in feedback uptake. AI literacy positively predicted trust (β = .46) and negatively predicted anxiety (β = -.39); trust was the strongest positive predictor of both engagement (β = .41) and uptake (β = .44), while anxiety exerted smaller negative effects. A cluster analysis identified three learner profiles - Confident Collaborators, Anxious Verifiers, and Detached Low-Literacy Users. Because anxiety was measured at three points across the period of AI-mediated collaboration, change over time was also examined: a repeated-measures ANOVA showed AI anxiety declining significantly across the three waves (partial η² = .18), and a latent growth curve model showed that higher AI literacy and higher trust each predicted a steeper decline. The qualitative findings showed that learners did not accept AI feedback uncritically but practised calibrated trust, verifying machine feedback against teachers and peers, and that AI literacy functioned as a regulating resource that tempered both over-reliance and anxiety. On this basis the study proposes a Calibrated Trust Framework for AI-mediated assessment, in which AI literacy supports calibrated trust, calibrated trust drives engagement, and engagement converts into uptake. The study advances a learner-centred account of human-AI collaboration in language assessment and argues that AI literacy, rather than tool sophistication alone, is central to responsible, pedagogically meaningful, AI-mediated assessment. Implications for assessment design, teacher education, and ethical practice are discussed.

items.title: Human-centered AI Capability and employee outcomes in an emerging economy: mediating role of empowerment and moderating role of digital culture
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in organizational life, yet whether and how this technology benefits employees remains poorly understood, particularly in emerging economies where digital transformation is proceeding rapidly but unevenly. Drawing on the Resource-Based View and Psychological Empowerment Theory, this study examines how organizational AI capability relates to employee performance and engagement and asks whether psychological empowerment channels this relationship and whether digital organizational culture strengthens or weakens it. Data were collected through a cross-sectional survey of 387 employees across 42 organizations in Egypt spanning the banking, telecommunications, healthcare, manufacturing, and retail sectors, and were analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling with bootstrapped mediation tests and multi-group comparisons. AI capability was positively associated with both employee performance and engagement, and employee empowerment partially mediated these relationships, indicating that AI's benefits for employees flow substantially through employees' sense of autonomy, competence, and impact rather than through technology alone. Digital organizational culture moderated this pathway: the AI capability-to-empowerment relationship was roughly twice as strong in organizations with a well-developed digital culture as in those without one. These findings extend the Resource-Based View to the individual level, position empowerment as a key psychological mechanism linking organizational AI resources to human outcomes and demonstrate that AI's human benefits are culturally and organizationally contingent rather than automatic. The results contribute emerging-economy evidence to a literature dominated by developed-country studies and offer practical guidance for organizations seeking to deploy AI in ways that empower, rather than sideline, their workforce.

items.title: Human-Centric HRC for Agriculture]{Design and Validation of a Human-Centric Human--Robot Collaboration System for Agriculture Using an AI-Driven Digital Twin
items.abstract: Abstract UK agriculture is facing an acute labour shortage, particularly on small farms where unpredictable and unstructured environments make automation difficult. Although robotic systems offer promising solutions, fully autonomous approaches remain costly and complex to implement. Human--Robot Collaboration provides a more practical alternative by combining human judgement with robotic assistance. This study investigates how digital twin-based simulation platforms can be designed to effectively model and optimise collaboration between humans and robots in complex agricultural settings. It also examines the performance trade-offs in vision and gesture-based collaboration systems, focusing on the balance between speed, accuracy and robustness, and explores the safety challenges related to recognising human intent and ensuring safe adaptive behaviour.To address these issues, a digital twin framework was constructed using the NVIDIA Omniverse platform, enabling the simulation of collaborative agricultural scenarios. The virtual testbed includes dynamic farm layouts, human models, and mobile robots equipped with RGB and LiDAR sensors to interpret gestures and actions with AI and a Vision-Language Model. Experimental results show high human detection accuracy (intersection over union up to 97%) and reliable robot responses to human guidance. This research presents the first virtual environment in agriculture that integrates human factors and intelligent robotic reasoning. The proposed framework provides a scalable, low-risk approach for developing, testing and optimising collaborative robotic systems, supporting wider adoption of intelligent automation in the farming sector.

items.title: Ignore the Writing: A Proposal for Peer Review in the Age of AI
items.abstract: The written paper has long stood in as proof of work: a fluent, well-structured manuscript was taken as evidence that good research lay behind it. Generative AI has broken that link. Polished manuscripts now cost nothing to produce, submissions are outgrowing what reviewers can absorb, and venues are turning to AI for help. The logical endpoint is a loop where AI writes the papers and AI reviews them. We argue that this loop is survivable, but only if it is given a reward function, and that human reviewing effort should become that reward function. We propose that submissions should consist of a 1500-word brief plus an unlimited, machine-verifiable appendix. Human reviewers judge whether a pursuit is worthwhile, models verify the experimental record in the appendix, and human curation decides where the field goes next.

items.title: Imagining Japanese Technofutures – The Role of Futurology and Science Fiction in Shaping the Information Society
items.abstract: The original roots of the information society (jōhō shakai) are clearly Japanese and date back to the year 1963. The concept was developed in the context of a private study group circle spearheaded by the anthropologist Umesao Tadao, including members like the science fiction writer Komatsu Sakyō and the futurologist Hayashi Yūjirō. Drawing on the methodology of science and technology studies (STS), I will show how the ideological narrative underlying Umesao’s original theory on the information industries was condensed into a sociotechnical imaginary (STI) in the years from 1963 to the end of the 1970s. This article explains why the narrative was so successful and how the Expo 1970 in Osaka served as a showcase for the public performance and stabilization of the STI. The article argues that this contributed to its lasting impact on the way in which Japanese technofutures were imagined, based on the premise of a techno-centered society.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Modern Software Development Lifecycle: Methodological Advancements, Developer Productivity, and Quality Engineering
items.abstract: The modern Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) is undergoing a profound paradigm shift driven by the rapid maturation of generative artificial intelligence, Large Language Models (LLMs), and automated program synthesis engines. While historical transitions—from linear Waterfall models to Agile sprints and continuous DevOps pipelines—focused primarily on procedural orchestration and organizational agility, the integration of Artificial Intelligence introduces cognitive automation directly into the engineering fabric. This research paper presents an exhaustive empirical and methodological investigation into the impact of AI across the end-to-end SDLC, evaluating its tangible ramifications on developer productivity, cognitive workflow dynamics, code quality engineering, and enterprise security. Employing a rigorous triangulated mixed-methods research design, this study combines: (i) quantitative repository mining across 1,200,000 commits spanning 45 enterprise software projects; (ii) a controlled randomized quasi-experiment comprising N = 120 professional software engineers measuring task velocity and cognitive workload via the NASA-TLX inventory; and (iii) longitudinal static analysis tracking post-release defect density and Common Weakness Enumerations (CWE). Our findings demonstrate that AI assistance compresses coding lead times by 55.8% and accelerates developer flow states, yielding substantial improvements across DORA deployment frequency and change velocity metrics. However, ungoverned AI code generation introduces acute quality paradoxes, including a 19.4% surge in code churn, subtle logic regression risks, and elevated vulnerabilities in insecure deserialization and unverified package dependencies. To resolve this tension, we propose a multi-tier Enterprise AI-Augmented SDLC (A-SDLC) Framework coupling Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) policy guardrails, local context retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), automated mutation test synthesis, and continuous AIOps observability. Finally, we analyze organizational governance imperatives, intellectual property licensing risks, and emerging horizons in autonomous multi-agent coding swarms, establishing an empirical blueprint for resilient, high-assurance software engineering.

items.abstract: Research Aim: This study aims to analyze the role of Artificial Intelligence in shaping inclusive leadership and to formulate strategies for strengthening local wisdom as a foundation for sustainable leadership. Design/Methods/Approach: The study employs a Literature Review approach, synthesizing scholarly works from Scopus, Web of Science, and Sinta (2010–2026). Thematic analysis is used to identify patterns and relationships among inclusive leadership, AI, and local wisdom. Research Finding: The findings reveal that inclusive leadership plays a critical role in bridging technological advancement and human values. It enhances employee engagement, innovation, and decision-making quality while mitigating algorithmic bias. Additionally, integrating local wisdom strengthens ethical governance, social legitimacy, and organizational sustainability through value-based and culturally grounded practices. Theoretical Contribution/Originality: This research offers a novel integrative framework combining AI, inclusive leadership, and local wisdom, addressing the gap between technological and humanistic perspectives in leadership studies. Practitioner/Policy Implication: The study provides strategic guidance for leaders and policymakers to implement human-centered AI, promote inclusivity, and embed cultural values into digital transformation. Research Limitation: This study relies on secondary data; future research should incorporate empirical validation and sector-specific analysis.

items.title: Infrastructure and its Discontents: Contestations of Power in Canada's AI Governance Scaffold
items.abstract: This paper develops a critical theoretical framework for understanding national Artificial Intelligence (AI) strategies through the lens of "Governance as Infrastructure." Integrating insights from Infrastructure Studies, Science and Technology Studies (STS), this paper employs Black Feminist Technoscience (BFTS) to reveal how AI governance infrastructures are assembled, maintained, and contested, and whose forms of knowledge, labour, and experience are rendered visible or invisible in these processes. We analyze the Canadian AI governance landscape through in-depth interviews with bureaucrats, civil society advocacy groups, academic researchers, and industry actors. Our inductive thematic analysis reveals how AI governance infrastructure enacts specific configurations of power, particularly through the politics of expertise; how actors navigate profound ambiguities related to AI's opacity, often involving strategic ignorance; and how mechanisms for justice and accountability struggle to address AI-related harms. We contend that a BFTS perspective highlights the limitations of current governance approaches and points toward alternative infrastructural designs prioritizing care, maintenance, participatory democracy, and adaptive temporalities to foster more equitable and accountable technology governance.

items.title: Intelligent Healthcare: AI and Machine Learning in Diagnosis, Precision Medicine, and the Pursuit of Explainable, Trustworthy Clinical Systems
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly used across healthcare to analyze complex clinical data, support diagnosis, guide precision medicine, accelerate drug discovery, and enable remote monitoring. This review examines established AI/ML techniques and their current clinical and commercial applications while considering the requirements for trustworthy adoption. Evidence reviewed across medical imaging, electronic health records, drug discovery, precision medicine, and remote patient monitoring shows broad use of supervised, unsupervised, deep-learning, hybrid, and ensemble approaches. Reported benefits include improved diagnostic and predictive performance, earlier risk identification, and support for individualized treatment. Recurring barriers include data privacy, model opacity, computational demands, algorithmic bias, limited external validation, workflow integration, and workforce readiness. Explainable AI, privacy-preserving learning, human-in-the-loop oversight, and evolving regulatory frameworks are prominent responses to these challenges. AI/ML is moving from experimental development toward practical healthcare use, but dependable adoption requires more than predictive accuracy. Robust external validation, transparent and interpretable models, privacy protection, equitable datasets, appropriate regulation, and effective clinician-AI collaboration are central to building trustworthy clinical systems.

Download the presentation first for a quick visual overview, then the full specification. The problem AI agents no longer just generate text. items.title: Key attributes for industry 4.0–enabled occupational safety and health management in modern methods of construction: a Delphi–VAHP approach
items.abstract: The adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies presents significant opportunities to enhance occupational safety and health (OSH) management within modern methods of construction (MMC). However, organisations often lack clarity on which factors are crucial for the adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies for OSH improvement in MMC. Existing studies have mainly investigated individual technologies, adoption barriers, or organisational capability factors, without systematically identifying and prioritising the comprehensive set of people, organisational, technological, and infrastructure attributes that enable effective Industry 4.0-enabled OSH management in MMC. This study addresses this gap by identifying, validating, and prioritising the key attributes for effective Industry 4.0-enabled OSH management in MMC using a four-stage methodological approach comprising SLR, expert verification, Delphi method, and voting analytic hierarchy process (VAHP). Through a combination of systematic literature review (SLR) and expert verification, 21 attributes were identified and grouped into four clusters: people, organisation, technology, and infrastructure. The 21 identified and validated attributes were then ranked by a group of experts through a two-round Delphi survey. Following this, the weights and importance of attributes were determined using the voting analytical hierarchy process (VAHP). The results indicate that organisation and people clusters achieved the highest relative priorities; Management support, workforce competence, and technology acceptance were identified as the highest-priority attributes. These findings reveal a sociotechnical hierarchy in which organisational and human capabilities are prioritised above technological and infrastructural capabilities, suggesting successful Industry 4.0-enabled transformation for OSH improvement depends more on social-subsystem capability than on technology deployment alone.

items.title: Leveraging Learning Analytics To Analyze Student Engagement And Learning Outcomes In Digital-Based Islamic Religious Education
items.abstract: Digital-based Islamic Religious Education (IRE) provides opportunities to use learning activity data to understand student engagement and learning outcomes. However, high levels of digital activity do not necessarily indicate deep cognitive engagement or successful learning. This study aims to analyze the use of learning analytics to examine student engagement and learning outcomes in digital-based IRE. It employs a qualitative approach using the library research method. Data were obtained by reviewing relevant literature on learning analytics, student engagement, learning outcomes, and digital-based IRE, and were analyzed descriptively through the identification and synthesis of findings. The results indicate that learning analytics can be used to identify behavioral engagement through access to learning materials, task completion, and participation in assessments, as well as to examine cognitive engagement through students’ understanding of learning materials and the quality of their responses. The use of these data can help educators identify learning difficulties, provide feedback, and determine appropriate instructional follow-up. Nevertheless, the relationship between engagement and learning outcomes must be interpreted cautiously because it is influenced by various factors. Digital activity data are also insufficient to assess all aspects of religious understanding and character development. This study concludes that learning analytics has the potential to support pedagogical decision-making in digital-based IRE, provided that data quality, privacy, and the learning context are taken into account.

items.title: Metacognition in the Era of Generative AI: Understanding Human Cognitive Engagement and AI Reliance
items.abstract: The growing integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into human cognitive activities, including problem-solving, decision-making, learning and information processing, has raised important questions about cognitive work allocation, metacognitive control and independent performance. Although GenAI can enhance efficiency by reducing cognitive demands, excessive reliance may weaken users’ engagement in reasoning, verification and independent task execution. This review examines the relationship between GenAI use and human cognition, with particular emphasis on cognitive offloading, appropriate reliance, over-reliance, automation bias and independent performance. Drawing on existing research, it explores how the effects of cognitive offloading depend on task characteristics and the distribution of cognitive responsibility between users and AI systems. The review further considers interventions such as think-first strategies, cognitive forcing functions, reflection, verification prompts and adaptive scaffolding that aim to preserve human cognitive engagement while benefiting from AI assistance. In addition, it examines behavioural telemetry including prompt intent, interaction timing, response editing and verification activities as a potential means of identifying patterns of engagement and reliance during multi-turn human AI interactions. These observable behaviours are treated as indirect indicators rather than definitive measures of internal cognitive processes. The review highlights the importance of evaluating not only task performance with AI assistance but also users’ ability to perform independently when such assistance is unavailable. It identifies a need for integrated frameworks that connect cognitive work allocation, metacognition, observable interaction patterns, reliance calibration and independent performance over time. Such frameworks may support the development of human-centred GenAI systems that improve task effectiveness while maintaining users’ critical thinking, self-regulation and cognitive autonomy.

items.title: Motivational organization in AI-supported writing: A self-determination perspective
items.abstract: This study examined how students’ motivational regulation during creative writing was organized when generative artificial intelligence (AI) was unavailable or optionally available. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT), motivation was conceptualized as configurations of intrinsic motivation, identified regulation, introjected regulation, and external regulation. The sample comprised 406 students in Grades 5–8 who completed comparable creative writing tasks without AI (Time 1) and with optional AI access (Time 2). Using a micro-longitudinal, person-centered design, latent profile analyses identified motivational configurations and examined psychological need satisfaction and academic achievement as predictors of profile membership; degree of AI use was examined at Time 2. Mean levels of motivational regulation remained largely stable, whereas person-centered analyses revealed heterogeneity in regulatory configurations and differences in the prevalence of comparable profiles. Autonomy satisfaction declined at Time 2, while higher need satisfaction, particularly autonomy and competence, was associated with more self-determined configurations. End-of-term grades differentiated profile membership at both occasions. Degree of AI use did not significantly predict profile membership. Cross-context analyses showed correspondence alongside redistribution. Because full profile similarity was unsupported, these patterns were interpreted descriptively rather than as transitions between equivalent latent states. AI availability coincided with configurational differences not apparent from mean-level analyses. The findings distinguish AI availability from usage intensity and suggest that AI-supported writing should be understood in relation to psychological needs, academic functioning, and regulatory demands surrounding support, delegation, authorship, and agency.

items.title: Motivations for social value creation in commercial buildings: evidence from New Zealand
items.abstract: Social value creation is a stated priority in commercial property and ESG agendas, yet little is known about why owners and occupiers pursue social initiatives or what sustains them. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT) and its sub-theory of organismic integration, this study examines the motivations underpinning social value in Auckland's prime office market, New Zealand. Eleven semi-structured interviews with eighteen owners, occupiers and agents across ten organisations were analysed thematically alongside corporate sustainability reporting. Motivations cluster around four drivers: market obligations, environmental imperatives, employee priorities and socio-cultural responsibilities. These range from external and introjected regulation through identified and integrated forms to, rarely, intrinsic motivation. Owners span the full range, whereas occupiers stabilise at identified regulation centred on employee well-being and organisational culture. This difference is positional rather than dispositional, since participants holding both roles express different motivations depending on the role from which they speak. Motivation also varies spatially: provision closest to the leasing transaction is the most externally regulated and provision furthest from it the most integrated. The study extends motivational theory to the commercial built environment, proposes a dual-stakeholder framework, and shows why assessments based on whether provision exists cannot distinguish durable from compliance-driven social value.

items.title: Organizational and ergonomic determinants of emotional exhaustion in functional diagnostics specialists: empirical justification of labor organization requirements
items.abstract: The presented work is devoted to the study of emotional exhaustion in functional diagnostics physicians in the context of organizational and ergonomic working conditions. The object of the research is emotional exhaustion as a basic component of professional burnout syndrome. The author examines in detail the specificity of the work of this professional group, which includes working in darkened rooms, forced static posture, high patient flow, and lack of micropauses. Special attention is paid to the fact that these factors have not yet been the subject of separate quantitative analysis. The paper analyzes the relationship between working conditions and the severity of emotional exhaustion, and substantiates the need to revise existing workload standards. The key emphasis is placed on the fact that emotional exhaustion in this category of specialists has not only a psychological, but also a pronounced organizational and environmental nature. A total of 228 functional diagnostics physicians were examined. The MBI questionnaire adapted by N.E. Vodopyanova, an author-developed questionnaire of somatic and sensory symptoms, and a brief questionnaire of organizational characteristics were used. Dispersion, correlation, and multiple regression analyses were applied. The scientific novelty of this study lies in the fact that it is the first to quantitatively assess the contribution of organizational factors to the development of emotional exhaustion in functional diagnostic physicians, as well as to compare objective workload parameters with the severity of sensory-muscular complaints. The relationship between the number of studies and the level of exhaustion is shown to be linear. The authors' key findings are as follows: with a workload of over 20 studies per day, the average exhaustion score reaches 32.1 ± 8.9, compared to 21.4 ± 8.7 with a workload of up to 10 studies. Continuous work without a microbreak for more than 60 minutes was found to increase exhaustion by 6.8 points. The strongest predictors were weekly workload (β = 0.31) and the duration of uninterrupted visual work (β = 0.27). Based on the data obtained, recommendations for optimizing the work regime were substantiated: no more than 15 examinations per shift, a mandatory five-minute break after each hour of work, and limiting continuous visual load to 45–50 minutes. These recommendations can be taken into account when developing local regulations for medical organizations.

items.title: Passive exposure to AI-generated text may reshape human academic writing through established cognitive mechanisms
items.abstract: This article is a hypothesis-generating perspective rather than a controlled study, and its claims should be read as propositions for testing. Large language models produce text with a recognizable linguistic signature that differs from much human academic prose in word choice, sentence shape, and discourse rhythm. We asked whether passive reading of artificial intelligence (AI)-associated text can change how people write, even when they never use a chatbot themselves. We defined passive exposure as reading text that carries AI-associated features without using an AI tool on one’s own writing, and we separated it from AI-assisted editing and hybrid human-AI authorship. The question grew from unsystematic expert observations made in teaching and editorial work, which motivate the hypothesis but do not test it. Large-scale corpus analyses show a sharp post-2022 rise in AI-associated vocabulary in published abstracts and in conference peer reviews. We organized the argument as one pathway running from exposure through internalization to convergence. The paper described candidate linguistic markers of AI text and explained how statistical and implicit learning, mere exposure and frequency effects, linguistic alignment, and experience-dependent neuroplasticity could carry the effect, although their application to AI text remains untested. We then considered what convergence would mean for assessment, stylistic diversity, and cognitive engagement, and we weighed alternative explanations, competing human input, and the confound with direct AI use. We closed with ten testable predictions, their practical limits, and propositions for writing education, so that the question can be studied while pre-AI baselines remain measurable.

items.title: PENERAPAN PROJECT BASED LEARNING BERBASIS CHROMEBOOK UNTUK MENINGKATKAN STUDENT ENGAGEMENT DALAM PEMBELAJARAN MENDALAM PENDIDIKAN PANCASILA KELAS VIII SMPN 13 MADIUN
items.abstract: Low student engagement remains one of the major challenges in Pancasila Education learning, as reflected in students' limited participation in discussions, lack of confidence in expressing ideas, and the suboptimal use of digital learning technology. This study aimed to describe the implementation of Chromebook-assisted Project Based Learning (PjBL), analyze its impact on improving student engagement, and explain its contribution to promoting Deep Learning in Pancasila Education. The study employed a Classroom Action Research (CAR) design based on the Kemmis and McTaggart model, consisting of two cycles: planning, action, observation, and reflection. The participants were 32 eighth-grade students of SMP Negeri 13 Madiun during the second semester of the 2025/2026 academic year. Data were collected through observations, questionnaires, and documentation, and analyzed using descriptive quantitative and qualitative techniques. The findings revealed that the implementation of Chromebook-assisted PjBL successfully improved students' engagement from 55.3% in the pre-cycle to 70.3% in Cycle I and 85.3% in Cycle II. Improvements were observed across behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement dimensions. Furthermore, integrating digital project activities through Chromebooks and the Dadu Nusantara learning media created learning experiences that were more mindful, meaningful, and joyful, thereby supporting the implementation of Deep Learning in Pancasila Education. These findings indicate that Chromebook-assisted Project Based Learning is an effective instructional approach for enhancing student engagement and improving the quality of learning in junior secondary schools.

items.title: Performance and moral trust in care robotics: ethical foundations for human–robot relationships
items.abstract: Abstract As global populations age and birth rates decline, many societies, especially in developed countries, face critical labor shortages in the caregiving sector. This demographic imbalance is straining existing care infrastructures and raising urgent questions about how to support an increasing number of elderly individuals who can no longer live independently. Socially interactive AI systems, particularly care robots, have emerged as a promising technological response. However, their successful integration into real-world care settings hinges on more than technical capability; it requires appropriately calibrated reliance on robotic performance and morally trustworthy sociotechnical care arrangements. This paper investigates the ethical and conceptual foundations of trust in human–robot interactions, with a focus on the caregiving context. Building on the distinction between performance trust and moral trust, we argue that its application to care robotics reveals an agency-trust mismatch: care robots are not moral agents, yet care contexts generate morally significant expectations concerning dignity, autonomy, privacy, non-deception, responsibility, and well-being. We therefore reconceptualize moral trust in care robotics as sociotechnical moral trust, directed not toward the robot alone but toward the broader care arrangement in which robotic behavior is designed, deployed, monitored, governed, and corrected by human and institutional actors. On this basis, we distinguish robot-level performance trust from system-level moral trustworthiness and derive ethical design and governance principles for trustworthy care-robotic systems.
